gloss: Something that causes great suffering to a lot of people.
examples: Malaria is still a *scourge* in much of the world.
Fentanyl has become the *scourge* of small towns across the state.
He called corruption the country's worst *scourge*.
contrast: Rhymes with *urge*: the -ge is a soft j sound, not a hard g.

gloss: A hurried, disorganized rush to get or do something.
examples: There was a mad *scramble* for the last few tickets.
The storm set off a *scramble* to board up windows.
Every December turns into a *scramble* to spend the budget.

gloss: A blank book that someone fills with photos, clippings, and keepsakes.
examples: She keeps a *scrapbook* of every trip they take.
The ticket stubs are glued into an old *scrapbook*.
My mother made *scrapbooks* for each of the grandchildren.

gloss: A shallow wound or mark made by rubbing against something rough.
examples: She came home with a *scrape* on her elbow.
There are a couple of *scrapes* on the rear bumper.
It's just a *scrape* — it'll heal in a few days.

gloss: A hand tool with a flat blade for removing something from a surface.
examples: Keep an ice *scraper* in the car all winter.
He took the old paint off with a *scraper*.
The set came with two putty knives and a *scraper*.

gloss: A loud, high cry made in fear, pain, or excitement.
examples: A *scream* came from the apartment upstairs.
We could hear *screams* from the roller coaster.
She let out a *scream* when the lights went off.

gloss: Someone who writes the scripts for movies or television.
examples: The *screenwriter* spent four years on the first draft.
She works in Los Angeles as a *screenwriter*.
Two *screenwriters* share credit on the film.
contrast: The w in *-writer* is silent: SKREEN-ry-tur.

gloss: A person whose job was to copy documents by hand before printing existed.
examples: Medieval *scribes* copied every book by hand.
The *scribe* recorded each name on a long list.
A single *scribe* could spend years on one manuscript.

gloss: A roll of paper or parchment with writing on it.
examples: The museum keeps the *scroll* under glass.
Ancient *scrolls* were stored in clay jars.
He unrolled the *scroll* carefully across the table.

gloss: The pouch of skin that holds the testicles.
examples: The testicles sit inside the *scrotum*.
The doctor checked the *scrotum* for swelling.
Any lump in the *scrotum* should be examined.
contrast: The plural is *scrotums* in everyday use, *scrota* in medical writing.

gloss: A moral feeling that stops someone from doing something wrong.
examples: He has no *scruples* about lying to customers.
Her *scruples* wouldn't let her keep the money.
They sold the company without a single *scruple*.

gloss: Careful and critical examination of someone or something.
examples: The deal came under intense *scrutiny* from regulators.
His numbers won't hold up to *scrutiny*.
The proposal deserves closer *scrutiny*.

gloss: A short, confused fight between people standing close together.
examples: A *scuffle* broke out near the exit.
Two fans were arrested after a *scuffle* in the stands.
The video shows a brief *scuffle* with security.

gloss: A disease caused by not getting enough vitamin C.
examples: Sailors once died of *scurvy* on long voyages.
Citrus fruit prevents *scurvy*.
*Scurvy* is rare today but still turns up in cases of poor diet.

gloss: A sailor, especially one of low rank in a navy or on a cargo ship.
examples: His grandfather was a merchant *seaman*.
Three *seamen* were rescued from the life raft.
The *seaman* had been at sea for eight months.
contrast: Irregular plural: *seamen*, not "seamans". It sounds just like *semen*.

gloss: A meeting at which people try to communicate with the dead.
examples: They held a *seance* in the old house on Halloween.
The medium charged fifty dollars for a *seance*.
Nobody at the *seance* would admit to being scared.
contrast: Often written *séance*. It is SAY-ahns, never "SEE-uhns".

gloss: A town or city with a harbor where ships load and unload.
examples: The city grew up around a busy *seaport*.
Most of the country's grain leaves through two *seaports*.
It was the largest *seaport* on the West Coast.

gloss: A painting or photograph of a view of the sea.
examples: A gray *seascape* hangs above the fireplace.
The gallery is full of *seascapes* and harbor scenes.
He paints *seascapes* in oil every summer.

gloss: The oily substance that skin produces naturally.
examples: Too much *sebum* can clog your pores.
The cleanser removes dirt and *sebum* without drying the skin.
Teenage skin usually makes more *sebum*.

gloss: The act of formally withdrawing from a country or organization.
examples: Eleven states voted for *secession* in 1861.
A small party still campaigns openly for *secession*.
Talk of *secession* comes back every few years.

gloss: The state of being kept away from other people.
examples: She spent her last years in *seclusion*.
The cabin offers complete *seclusion*.
He lives in *seclusion* on a farm upstate.

gloss: The practice of keeping something hidden from other people.
examples: The talks were held in complete *secrecy*.
The company's *secrecy* about the recall angered customers.
Jurors are sworn to *secrecy*.

gloss: A piece of information kept hidden from other people.
examples: Can you keep a *secret*?
She told me her family's biggest *secret*.
Half the town knew the *secret* by Monday.

gloss: The permanent office and staff that run a large organization.
examples: The *secretariat* released its annual report in June.
She has worked at the *secretariat* in Geneva for a decade.
The *secretariat* handles the day-to-day business of the union.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The process by which a gland produces a fluid, or the fluid itself.
examples: Insulin *secretion* drops in people with diabetes.
The plant's sticky *secretion* traps insects.
The lab tested *secretions* from the wound.

gloss: A large sofa made of separate pieces that fit together.
examples: We bought a gray *sectional* for the living room.
The *sectional* takes up half the basement.
Their new *sectional* has a recliner built into one end.

gloss: The principle that government and public life should stay separate from religion.
examples: *Secularism* is written into the constitution.
The debate is really about *secularism* in the schools.
French *secularism* keeps religious symbols out of classrooms.

gloss: The use of drugs to make a patient calm or sleepy for a procedure.
examples: The procedure is done under light *sedation*.
He was kept under *sedation* for two days.
The dentist offers *sedation* for nervous patients.

gloss: A drug that makes someone calmer or sleepy.
examples: The vet gave the dog a mild *sedative*.
She takes a *sedative* before long flights.
*Sedatives* can be habit-forming.

gloss: The ritual family meal held on the first nights of Passover.
examples: We're hosting the *seder* at our house this year.
Her family's *seder* runs past midnight.
He was invited to a friend's *seder* for the first time.
contrast: The first vowel is the one in *say*: SAY-dur.

gloss: Speech or action that encourages people to rebel against their government.
examples: Two of the organizers were charged with *sedition*.
Under the old law, criticizing the king counted as *sedition*.
Prosecutors called the plot nothing short of *sedition*.

gloss: The act of tempting someone into sex or into something attractive but unwise.
examples: The novel is a story of *seduction* and betrayal.
He mistook her friendliness for *seduction*.
The whole ad rests on the *seduction* of easy money.

gloss: A person who is looking for something.
examples: Job *seekers* lined up around the block.
The country took in thousands of asylum *seekers*.
The site matches *seekers* with local employers.

gloss: The slow leaking of liquid through small openings.
examples: There's *seepage* in the basement after heavy rain.
Crews are still trying to stop the *seepage* from the tank.
Water *seepage* weakened the foundation.

gloss: A smooth transition from one topic, scene, or song to the next.
examples: That's a nice *segue* into our next story.
The DJ's *segue* between the two tracks was seamless.
He was looking for a *segue* to change the subject.
contrast: Spelled like Italian but said SEG-way — the same sound as the *Segway* scooter.

gloss: The habit of caring only about yourself.
examples: His *selfishness* finally cost him the friendship.
She accused the company of pure *selfishness*.
There's a difference between *selfishness* and self-care.

gloss: The quality of putting other people's needs before your own.
examples: The nurses were honored for their *selflessness*.
Her *selflessness* during the flood saved two families.
He talks about service with real *selflessness*.

gloss: The study of meaning in language, or an argument about the exact meaning of words.
examples: That's just *semantics* — the result is the same either way.
We wasted an hour arguing over *semantics*.
*Semantics* is one branch of linguistics.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: "*Semantics* is...", not "are".

gloss: An appearance or trace of something, often not the real thing.
examples: Power came back and life returned to some *semblance* of normal.
The talks gave at least a *semblance* of progress.
She kept up a *semblance* of calm until the door closed.

gloss: The fluid containing sperm produced by male reproductive organs.
examples: The lab analyzed a *semen* sample.
*Semen* is checked for sperm count and movement.
The clinic freezes and stores *semen* for years.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *seamen*, the plural of *seaman*.

gloss: A competitor who has reached the round just before the final.
examples: She was a *semifinalist* at the national spelling bee.
Four *semifinalists* are left in the tournament.
Every *semifinalist* gets a small cash prize.

gloss: A college that trains people to become priests, ministers, or rabbis.
examples: He left law school for a *seminary* in Boston.
The *seminary* has about two hundred students.
Several *seminaries* have closed in the last decade.

gloss: The long trailer pulled by a truck cab, or the whole truck and trailer.
examples: A *semitrailer* jackknifed across two lanes.
The *semitrailer* was hauling frozen food.
Two *semitrailers* were parked behind the warehouse.
contrast: In speech Americans usually shorten it to a *semi* (SEM-eye).

gloss: A coarse wheat flour used for pasta and porridge.
examples: Good dry pasta is made from durum *semolina*.
She dusts the pizza peel with *semolina*.
*Semolina* pudding was a childhood breakfast for him.

gloss: The loss of memory and mental sharpness that can come with old age.
examples: The family mistook early dementia for ordinary *senility*.
He jokes about his approaching *senility*.
*Senility* is an old-fashioned word for what doctors now call dementia.

gloss: The rank or advantage that comes from having worked somewhere longer.
examples: Shifts are assigned by *seniority*.
She has enough *seniority* to pick her vacation weeks.
The layoffs followed strict *seniority* rules.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A physical feeling, or a person or thing that causes great excitement.
examples: He felt a burning *sensation* in his throat.
She lost all *sensation* in her left hand.
The rookie pitcher was an overnight *sensation*.

gloss: A person's feelings and sense of what is right or in good taste.
examples: The ad offended some viewers' *sensibilities*.
He brings a designer's *sensibility* to the project.
The show's humor fits modern *sensibilities*.
contrast: *Sensibility* is about taste and feeling; being *sensible* means being practical.

gloss: The quality of appealing strongly to the physical senses.
examples: Critics praised the film for its quiet *sensuality*.
There's a warm *sensuality* to her singing.
The painting's *sensuality* shocked audiences at the time.

gloss: The ability to feel and to be aware of one's own experience.
examples: Researchers still argue about animal *sentience*.
No serious scientist claims the chatbot has *sentience*.
The law now recognizes the *sentience* of octopuses.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The act of keeping things apart, or a period when a married couple lives apart.
examples: The country is built on the *separation* of church and state.
They agreed to a trial *separation* last spring.
The *separation* of the recycling is done at the plant.

gloss: Someone who wants their region to break away and form its own country.
examples: *Separatists* control the eastern provinces.
The *separatist* movement lost its last referendum.
Government troops clashed with armed *separatists*.

gloss: A brownish tone, especially of old photographs.
examples: The wedding photos have faded to *sepia*.
The app can add a *sepia* filter with one tap.
Everything in the album is printed in *sepia*.

gloss: A dangerous reaction of the whole body to an infection.
examples: She nearly died of *sepsis* after surgery.
*Sepsis* kills thousands of hospital patients every year.
The nurses watched him closely for signs of *sepsis*.

gloss: The wall of cartilage that divides the two sides of the nose.
examples: He broke his nose and has a deviated *septum*.
Surgery straightened her *septum* and fixed the snoring.
A ring through the *septum* is a common piercing now.
contrast: The plural is *septa*, not "septums".

gloss: A set of things that follow one another in a particular order.
examples: Enter the numbers in the right *sequence*.
The opening *sequence* of the movie is famous.
Scientists mapped the whole DNA *sequence*.

gloss: A giant evergreen tree that grows in California and can live thousands of years.
examples: Some of these *sequoias* were already old before Rome fell.
A fallen *sequoia* blocked the trail for a month.
Standing under a *sequoia* makes you feel very small.

gloss: Music performed for someone, especially outdoors by a lover at night.
examples: He sang a *serenade* under her window.
The mariachi band played a *serenade* for the couple.
Mozart wrote a number of *serenades* for small ensembles.

gloss: The luck of finding something good without looking for it.
examples: Their meeting was pure *serendipity*.
A lot of scientific discovery comes down to *serendipity*.
I found the apartment by sheer *serendipity*.

gloss: The system in which peasants were legally bound to a landowner's land.
examples: *Serfdom* was abolished in Russia in 1861.
The peasants lived in something close to *serfdom*.
Historians still argue about how *serfdom* finally ended.
contrast: The first syllable sounds exactly like *surf*.

gloss: The quality of being serious or grave.
examples: He doesn't grasp the *seriousness* of the charges.
The doctor explained the *seriousness* of the diagnosis.
She said it with complete *seriousness*.

gloss: A chemical in the brain that affects mood, sleep, and appetite.
examples: The drug raises *serotonin* levels in the brain.
Sunlight is linked to *serotonin* production.
Low *serotonin* may play a part in depression.

gloss: A person employed to do household work in someone else's home.
examples: The estate once employed a dozen *servants*.
A *servant* answered the door and took his coat.
In the novel the *servants* live on the top floor.

gloss: A man serving in the armed forces.
examples: The bill raises pay for *servicemen* and women.
A young *serviceman* was honored before the game.
Thousands of *servicemen* came home that spring.
contrast: Irregular plural: *servicemen*, not "servicemans".

gloss: The condition of being forced to work for someone with no freedom.
examples: Many colonists arrived under indentured *servitude*.
The workers described conditions close to *servitude*.
The Constitution outlaws involuntary *servitude*.

gloss: How serious, harsh, or bad something is.
examples: Treatment depends on the *severity* of the injury.
Nobody expected the *severity* of the storm.
The *severity* of the sentence surprised the courtroom.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Physical intimacy between people, or the category of male or female.
examples: The form asks for your name, age, and *sex*.
Schools here teach *sex* education in ninth grade.
Both *sexes* were represented on the panel.

gloss: A metal ring locked around a prisoner's wrist or ankle.
examples: The prisoner shuffled into court in *shackles*.
Guards removed his *shackles* before the hearing.
The museum displays *shackles* from a slave ship.

gloss: A soft rock that splits into thin layers and often holds oil or gas.
examples: The boom in *shale* changed the state's economy.
They drill through hundreds of feet of *shale*.
*Shale* gas turned the country into an exporter.

gloss: The quality of lacking depth, either physically or in thought.
examples: The *shallowness* of the river lets you wade across.
He was criticized for the *shallowness* of his argument.
The show makes fun of the *shallowness* of celebrity culture.

gloss: A healer who is believed to communicate with spirits.
examples: The village *shaman* led the ceremony.
*Shamans* often use drums and chanting.
He spent a year studying with a *shaman* in Siberia.

gloss: A state of complete disorder or ruin.
examples: The kitchen was a *shambles* after the party.
Their finances are in *shambles*.
The whole project turned into a *shambles*.
contrast: Always ends in -s but takes a singular verb: "The place *is* a shambles."

gloss: A settlement of rough huts built by poor people on the edge of a city.
examples: A *shantytown* grew up along the railroad tracks.
Families in the *shantytown* have no running water.
The city cleared two *shantytowns* last year.

gloss: A sharp broken piece of glass, pottery, or metal.
examples: *Shards* of glass covered the sidewalk.
She cut her foot on a *shard* from the broken bowl.
Archaeologists pieced together *shards* of a clay jar.

gloss: The quality of having a fine cutting edge, a clear image, or a harsh tone.
examples: Test the *sharpness* of the blade on a sheet of paper.
The new lens gives remarkable *sharpness*.
There was a *sharpness* in her voice that ended the conversation.

gloss: Someone who shoots very accurately, with a gun or at a basket.
examples: Police *sharpshooters* took positions on the roof.
He was a *sharpshooter* in the army.
The team traded for a *sharpshooter* off the bench.

gloss: A close-fitting cover for a knife blade or something long and thin.
examples: He slid the knife back into its *sheath*.
The cable has a tough plastic *sheath*.
Each nerve is wrapped in a protective *sheath*.
contrast: The noun *sheath* ends in an unvoiced th; the verb *sheathe* ends in a voiced one.

gloss: Everything that is involved in something, used mainly in the phrase the whole shebang.
examples: For a hundred bucks you get the whole *shebang*.
They booked the hall, the caterer, the band, the whole *shebang*.
He sold the house, the truck, the whole *shebang*.
contrast: Used almost only in the fixed phrase *the whole shebang*.

gloss: A hard varnish made from resin and brushed onto wood.
examples: Two coats of *shellac* sealed the tabletop.
The old finish is *shellac*, not polyurethane.
*Shellac* dries in about half an hour.
contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: shuh-LAK.

gloss: A brown Asian mushroom with a meaty flavor, widely used in cooking.
examples: Add sliced *shiitakes* to the broth at the end.
*Shiitake* mushrooms are grown on hardwood logs.
The soup has tofu, scallions, and *shiitake*.
contrast: Three syllables: shee-TAH-kee, not "shy-take".

gloss: Someone who secretly promotes a product or person while pretending to be an ordinary supporter.
examples: The glowing reviewer turned out to be a *shill* for the company.
Critics called him a *shill* for the oil industry.
Auction *shills* bid to drive the price up.

gloss: A soft, wavering light or gleam.
examples: There was a *shimmer* of heat above the highway.
The lake had a silver *shimmer* at dusk.
The eyeshadow leaves a light *shimmer*.

gloss: The industry of designing and constructing ships.
examples: *Shipbuilding* was the town's main employer for a century.
The country invested heavily in *shipbuilding*.
He studied naval architecture and went into *shipbuilding*.

gloss: A company or person that sends goods, or arranges for them to be sent.
examples: The *shipper* pays for insurance on the load.
Large *shippers* negotiate much lower rates.
Contact the *shipper* if the package never arrives.

gloss: A place where ships are built or repaired.
examples: His father worked in the *shipyard* for thirty years.
The *shipyard* laid off half its workers.
Two destroyers are being repaired at the *shipyard*.

gloss: A shoelace, or, in the phrase on a shoestring, a very small amount of money.
examples: The whole movie was made on a *shoestring*.
He tripped over a loose *shoestring*.
They run the shelter on a *shoestring* budget.

gloss: A person who fires a gun, or a player who shoots at the basket or goal.
examples: Police identified the *shooter* within hours.
He's the best three-point *shooter* on the team.
The *shooter* was arrested two blocks away.

gloss: An incident in which someone is shot.
examples: There was a *shooting* downtown last night.
The city has seen fewer *shootings* this year.
He watched the *shooting* from his window.

gloss: Someone who shops far more than they need to or can afford.
examples: She jokes that she's a hopeless *shopaholic*.
The book is a comedy about a *shopaholic* in debt.
*Shopaholics* tend to hide the receipts.

gloss: A crumbly cookie made with a lot of butter and very few ingredients.
examples: She bakes *shortbread* every Christmas.
The tin of *shortbread* was empty by noon.
Real *shortbread* has only three ingredients.

gloss: A sweet biscuit-like cake served with fruit and whipped cream.
examples: Strawberry *shortcake* is the classic summer dessert here.
She baked individual *shortcakes* for each guest.
The *shortcake* was still warm from the oven.

gloss: Solid vegetable fat used to make pastry and cookies tender.
examples: The recipe calls for a cup of *shortening*.
You can use butter instead of *shortening*.
*Shortening* is what keeps the crust flaky.
contrast: In the kitchen this is a solid fat, not the act of making something shorter.

gloss: A fast way of writing using symbols, or a short way of referring to something bigger.
examples: Court reporters once took everything down in *shorthand*.
"Wall Street" is *shorthand* for the finance industry.
She uses her own *shorthand* in meetings.

gloss: The state of being short, especially of breath.
examples: *Shortness* of breath is a common symptom.
Call a doctor if you have chest pain or *shortness* of breath.
The *shortness* of the meeting surprised everyone.

ru: шортстоп (игрок между 2-й и 3-й базой в бейсболе)
gloss: The baseball fielder who plays between second and third base.
examples: The *shortstop* made a diving catch.
He played *shortstop* all through high school.
Good *shortstops* have quick hands and a strong arm.

gloss: A tiny torn piece, or the smallest possible amount of something.
examples: There isn't a *shred* of evidence against her.
The dog tore the pillow to *shreds*.
*Shreds* of paper were all over the floor.

gloss: A machine that cuts paper or waste into thin strips.
examples: Run the old bank statements through the *shredder*.
The office *shredder* jammed again.
We rented a *shredder* for the yard waste.

gloss: A tiny mouse-like animal with a long pointed snout.
examples: A *shrew* darted under the woodpile.
*Shrews* have to eat almost constantly.
The cat left a dead *shrew* on the porch.

gloss: A quick raising of the shoulders to show you don't know or don't care.
examples: He answered with a *shrug*.
She gave a small *shrug* and walked away.
The announcement was met with *shrugs*.

gloss: A mixing of playing cards, or a slow dragging way of walking.
examples: Give the deck a good *shuffle* before you deal.
You could hear the *shuffle* of feet in the hallway.
He crossed the room with a tired *shuffle*.

gloss: A game in which players slide weighted disks along a long smooth surface.
examples: They play *shuffleboard* at the bar every Thursday.
The cruise ship has a *shuffleboard* court on the top deck.
My grandparents took *shuffleboard* very seriously.

gloss: The state of being ill, or a feeling of nausea.
examples: He missed a week of work with *sickness*.
Motion *sickness* ruined the drive up the mountain.
There's been a lot of *sickness* in the family this winter.

gloss: A column of extra material beside the main text or web page.
examples: The menu is in the *sidebar* on the left.
The article has a *sidebar* explaining how to apply.
You can hide the *sidebar* for more room.

gloss: A small one-wheeled car attached to the side of a motorcycle for a passenger.
examples: His dog rides in the *sidecar* with goggles on.
The old motorcycle came with a *sidecar*.
You almost never see *sidecars* on the highway anymore.

gloss: A small extra attraction at a fair, or something unimportant that distracts from the main issue.
examples: The fight over the logo was a *sideshow*.
The circus had a *sideshow* with a fortune teller.
Reporters treated the scandal as a *sideshow* to the election.

gloss: A short nap taken in the early afternoon.
examples: He takes a *siesta* after lunch every day.
The shops close for a two-hour *siesta*.
A quick *siesta* got her through the evening shift.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The ability to see, or something that is seen.
examples: He lost the *sight* in one eye.
The sunset over the bay was a beautiful *sight*.
We saw all the *sights* of the city in one day.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *site* and *cite* — three different words.

gloss: An occasion when someone sees something rare or unexpected.
examples: There have been three bear *sightings* this month.
The *sighting* was reported to the sheriff's office.
A rare bird *sighting* drew a crowd of photographers.

gloss: A board with words or a picture that gives information, or an indication that something exists.
examples: The *sign* says the store closes at nine.
A high fever can be a *sign* of infection.
Somebody knocked down the stop *sign* on the corner.
contrast: The g is silent — SYN — but it comes back in *signal* and *signature*.

gloss: The signs in a place, taken all together.
examples: The airport's *signage* is confusing.
New *signage* went up along the trail.
The store spent thousands on *signage*.

gloss: The importance or deeper meaning of something.
examples: Historians still debate the *significance* of the treaty.
The date has personal *significance* for her.
The difference had no statistical *significance*.

gloss: A device fitted to a gun to make it quieter.
examples: The pistol had a *silencer* screwed onto the barrel.
*Silencers* are illegal in several states.
A real *silencer* is far louder than the ones in movies.
contrast: In British English *silencer* also means a car's *muffler*; Americans use *muffler* for that.

gloss: A hard mineral found in sand and quartz, used to make glass.
examples: Every shoebox comes with a little packet of *silica* gel.
Workers who cut stone breathe in *silica* dust.
Glass is made mostly of melted *silica*.
contrast: *Silica* is the mineral, *silicon* the element, and *silicone* the rubbery synthetic.
